03.01.title: Functions of several variables
03.01.html:
Real quantities depend on more than one thing. Gas pressure depends on temperature and volume; the stress in a beam depends on position along it and across it; the temperature of a plate depends on x, y and time. This lesson sets up the language: level sets to see such functions, partial derivatives to measure them, and the total differential to estimate how errors and changes combine.

Seeing a function of two variables

f(x,y) is a surface over the plane. Two views help:

  • Level sets (contours): the curves f(x,y)=c. A weather map’s isobars, a topographic map’s height lines, isotherms on a heated plate.
  • Slices: hold one variable fixed and plot f against the other. A slice is an ordinary one-variable function.

Partial derivatives

The partial derivative with respect to x is the slope of the slice in the x direction, with y held fixed:

∂x∂f​(x,y)=h→0lim​hf(x+h,y)−f(x,y)​.

Compute it by treating every other variable as a constant. Numerically, use the central difference from lesson 01.03 in one variable at a time.

The total differential

If both inputs change a little, the changes add up to first order:

df=∂x∂f​dx+∂y∂f​dy.

This is the tangent-plane approximation, the 2D version of the tangent line. Two uses dominate engineering:

  1. Sensitivity: which input matters most? Compare ∣∂f/∂xi​∣Δxi​ term by term.
  2. Error propagation: for independent random errors σi​, σf​≈∑i​(∂f/∂xi​)2σi2​​.

Order of differentiation

For smooth functions, ∂2f/∂x∂y=∂2f/∂y∂x (Schwarz’s theorem). The code checks it numerically.

Worked examplePressure in a heated tank

1 kg of air (R=287 J/(kg K)) at T=300 K in V=0.5 m³. Ideal gas: p=mRT/V=172.2 kPa.

  1. ∂p/∂T=mR/V=574 Pa/K.
  2. ∂p/∂V=−mRT/V2=−344400 Pa/m³.
  3. The tank warms by 2 K and bulges by 0.01 m³: dp=574⋅2−344400⋅0.01=1148−3444=−2296 Pa.
  4. Exact: p(302,0.51)−p(300,0.5)=169949−172200=−2251 Pa. The linear estimate is 2% off because dV/V=2% isn’t tiny.
  5. Error propagation: with σT​=0.5 K and σV​=0.002 m³, σp​=(574⋅0.5)2+(344400⋅0.002)2​, which is 2872+6892​=746 Pa. The volume measurement dominates, so that’s the one to improve.

Exercise 1Which measurement matters?

The bending stress in a rectangular beam is σ=6M/(bh2). With M=2 kN m, b=40 mm, h=100 mm, each measured with 1% error, which dimension dominates the uncertainty in σ?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. σ=6⋅2×106/(40⋅1002)=30 MPa.
  2. Relative sensitivities: ∂M∂σ​σM​=1, ∂b∂σ​σb​=−1, ∂h∂σ​σh​=−2.
  3. 1% errors become 1%, 1% and 2% in σ; combined 1+1+4​=2.4%, about 0.73 MPa.
  4. The depth h dominates because it appears squared. Measure it more carefully first.

03.02.title: The gradient
03.02.html:
The gradient packs all the partial derivatives into one vector, and that vector has a meaning you can see: it points uphill, as steeply as possible, perpendicular to the contours. Heat flows against the temperature gradient, fluid accelerates down the pressure gradient, and optimisers walk against the gradient of the cost. This lesson builds all three ideas from one formula.

Definition and directional derivatives

∇f=(∂x∂f​,∂y∂f​,∂z∂f​).

The rate of change of f in the direction of a unit vector u is the directional derivative

Du​f=∇f⋅u=∣∇f∣cosθ.

It’s largest when u points along ∇f (rate ∣∇f∣), zero when u is perpendicular to it (moving along a contour), and most negative straight against it.

Gradients in physics

  • Fourier’s law: heat flux q=−k∇T. Heat runs downhill in temperature, fastest where the isotherms crowd together.
  • Pressure force: a fluid parcel feels −∇p per unit volume.
  • Conservative forces: F=−∇V for a potential energy V (more in lesson 03.07).

Gradient descent

To minimise f, step against the gradient: xk+1​=xk​−η∇f(xk​). For the quadratic bowl f=21​xTAx, the gradient is Ax and each step multiplies the error in eigen-direction i by 1−ηλi​. So:

  • The step must satisfy η<2/λmax​, or the steepest direction blows up.
  • With the best fixed step, the error shrinks by κ+1κ−1​ per step, where κ=λmax​/λmin​. Long, narrow valleys (large κ) make gradient descent zigzag and crawl.

That’s the same condition number from Phase 02, and it’s why CG (lesson 02.15) and Newton’s method (03.03) beat plain descent.

Worked exampleHeat flow on a plate

A plate has temperature T(x,y)=100−2x2−y2 °C, with x,y in metres, and conductivity k=50 W/(m K).

  1. ∇T=(−4x,−2y). At (1,2): ∇T=(−4,−4) °C/m.
  2. Rate of change heading in direction (3,4)/5: Du​T=−4⋅0.6−4⋅0.8=−5.6 °C/m.
  3. Steepest increase: along (−1,−1)/2​, towards the hot centre, at ∣∇T∣=42​=5.66 °C/m.
  4. Heat flux: q=−k∇T=(200,200) W/m², magnitude 283 W/m², pointing away from the centre.
  5. Check perpendicularity: the isotherm through (1,2) is 2x2+y2=6, with tangent direction (−y,2x)=(−2,2). Its dot product with ∇T=(−4,−4) is 8−8=0.

  3. Slope =∣∇z∣=0.42​=0.566, a 56.6% grade (about 29.5∘). Steep: that’s a black ski run.

03.03.title: Multivariable Taylor and the Hessian
03.03.html:
Near a point, a smooth function of several variables looks like a constant plus a tilted plane plus a curved bowl, saddle or dome. The tilt is the gradient; the curvature is the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives. Its eigenvalues tell you whether a stationary point is a minimum, maximum or saddle, which is exactly the stability test for equilibria in mechanics.

The second-order expansion

f(x+h)≈f(x)+∇f(x)⋅h+21​hTH(x)h,Hij​=∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​.

H is symmetric for smooth f (lesson 03.01), so the spectral theorem (02.10) applies: in the eigenvector directions, the quadratic term is a sum of independent parabolas 21​λi​ci2​.

Classifying stationary points

At a stationary point ∇f=0, and the Hessian decides:

Eigenvalues of H Shape Type
all positive bowl local minimum
all negative dome local maximum
mixed signs saddle neither
some zero flat direction the test is inconclusive

In mechanics, an equilibrium is stable when the potential energy has a minimum there: H positive definite (lesson 02.11). A ball on a saddle-shaped surface is in equilibrium but unstable.

Newton’s method in several variables

Minimise the quadratic model instead of f: set its gradient to zero, ∇f+Hh=0, and solve for the step

Hh=−∇f.

Near a minimum with positive definite H, this converges quadratically, like the 1D Newton method in lesson 01.05, and it doesn’t care how elongated the bowl is. The cost is forming and solving with H each step.

Worked exampleFind and classify

f(x,y)=x3−3x+y2.

  1. ∇f=(3x2−3, 2y)=0 at (1,0) and (−1,0).
  2. H=(6x0​02​).
  3. At (1,0): eigenvalues 6 and 2, both positive, so a minimum with f=−2.
  4. At (−1,0): eigenvalues −6 and 2, a saddle with f=2. It’s a maximum along x and a minimum along y.
  5. Quadratic model at the minimum: f≈−2+3(x−1)2+y2. At (1.1,0.1) it gives −1.960; the exact value is 1.331−3.3+0.01=−1.959.

Exercise 1Stability of a spring-loaded hinge

A bar of length L hinged at its base is held upright by a torsional spring kt​ and loaded by a vertical force P at its tip. The potential energy is V(θ)=21​kt​θ2+PLcosθ. When is the upright position θ=0 stable?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V′(θ)=kt​θ−PLsinθ, which is zero at θ=0: an equilibrium for every load.
  2. V′′(0)=kt​−PL.
  3. Stable (a minimum) when kt​−PL>0, so P<kt​/L. The critical load Pcr​=kt​/L is a buckling load, the 1D version of the Euler column in Phase 06.
  4. Above it, V′′(0)<0: the upright position becomes a maximum and the bar tips over to a bent equilibrium.

03.04.title: Constrained optimisation
03.04.html:
Design is optimisation with rules: the lightest bracket that doesn’t yield, the cheapest tank that holds 1000 litres, the strongest beam that fits in a given depth. Lagrange multipliers turn “optimise f subject to g=0” into a system of equations, and the multiplier itself has a meaning engineers use constantly: the price of the constraint.

The geometric condition

At a constrained optimum you can’t improve f by sliding along the constraint curve g=0. So the gradient of f has no component along the curve: it’s perpendicular to it, just like ∇g. The two gradients are parallel:

∇f=λ∇g,g(x)=0.

Equivalently, look for stationary points of the Lagrangian L(x,λ)=f(x)−λg(x) in all variables, x and λ together.

What the multiplier means

If the constraint is g(x)=c and you relax c a little, the optimal value changes at the rate

dcdf∗​=λ.

That’s a shadow price: how much more performance you’d buy per unit of loosened constraint. In mechanics, multipliers are the reaction forces: minimise energy subject to “this node doesn’t move”, and λ is the support force.

Inequalities

Real constraints are often inequalities (σ≤σallow​). The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions extend Lagrange: either the constraint is inactive and its multiplier is zero, or it’s active and behaves like an equality. Lesson 04.19 builds a solver for them.

Worked exampleThe cheapest can

Make a closed cylinder holding V=1 litre with the least sheet metal. Area A=2πr2+2πrh; constraint πr2h=V.

  1. ∂A/∂r=4πr+2πh=λ2πrh and ∂A/∂h=2πr=λπr2.
  2. The second equation gives λ=2/r. Substitute into the first: 4πr+2πh=4πh, so h=2r. The height equals the diameter.
  3. With V=10−3 m³: 2πr3=V gives r=54.19 mm and h=108.4 mm.
  4. Area: A=6πr2=0.05536 m² =553.6 cm².
  5. Multiplier: λ=2/r=36.9 m⁻¹. One more millilitre (10−6 m³) costs 36.9×10−6 m² =0.37 cm² of extra sheet.

Real cans are taller than this because the lids are thicker, seamed, and more expensive per area than the wall. Put that cost into A and the optimum shifts.

Exercise 1The strongest beam from a log

A rectangular beam of width b and depth h is cut from a round log of diameter D, so b2+h2=D2. Bending strength is proportional to the section modulus bh2/6. Find the best ratio h/b.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Maximise bh2 subject to b2+h2=D2. Lagrange: h2=2λb and 2bh=2λh, so λ=b and h2=2b2.
  2. h/b=2​≈1.41.
  3. From the constraint: b=D/3​=0.577D and h=2/3​D=0.816D.
  4. This is the classic result Parent derived in 1708, and close to the proportions of standard sawn timber joists.

03.05.title: Double and triple integrals
03.05.html:
Mass, centroid, second moment of area, total heat in a body: all are integrals over a region in 2D or 3D. You compute them as iterated one-dimensional integrals, slicing the region into strips. The second moment of area I is the headline example in mechanics, because it sets how stiff a beam is in bending.

Iterated integrals

Over a rectangle, integrate in one variable with the other fixed, then integrate the result:

∬R​fdA=∫ab​(∫cd​f(x,y)dy)dx.

For a non-rectangular region, the inner limits depend on the outer variable: for the region between y=g1​(x) and y=g2​(x), the inner integral runs from g1​(x) to g2​(x). Fubini’s theorem says the order doesn’t matter for well-behaved f, so pick whichever makes the limits easiest.

Quantities you’ll compute

Quantity Integral
Area A=∬dA
Centroid yˉ​=A1​∬ydA
Second moment about the x axis Ix​=∬y2dA
Mass of a body m=∭ρdV

For a rectangle of width b and height h about its centroid, I=∫−h/2h/2​by2dy=bh3/12. The cube on h is why beams are deep rather than wide.

The parallel axis theorem

The second moment about an axis a distance d from the centroid is I=Ic​+Ad2. Build composite sections (T, I, channel) from rectangles with it.

Numerical integration in 2D

The midpoint rule extends directly: split the region into cells, evaluate at each centre, sum value × area. Its error is O(h2) as in 1D. For high dimensions, grids become hopeless (nd points) and Monte Carlo (average f at random points) wins: its error falls like 1/N​ regardless of dimension.

Worked exampleBending stiffness of a T-beam

Flange 100×20 mm on top of a web 20×80 mm, base at y=0.

  1. Areas: flange 2000 mm² with centroid at y=90; web 1600 mm² at y=40.
  2. Centroid: yˉ​=(2000⋅90+1600⋅40)/3600=67.78 mm.
  3. Flange: Ic​=100⋅203/12=66667, distance d=22.22, Ad2=987654. Total 1054321 mm⁴.
  4. Web: Ic​=20⋅803/12=853333, d=27.78, Ad2=1234568. Total 2087901 mm⁴.
  5. I=3.142×106 mm⁴. The code gets the same number by brute-force double integration over the shape.

A solid 40×100 mm rectangle (more material, 4000 mm²) has I=40⋅1003/12=3.333×106 mm⁴. The T uses 10% less material for 6% less stiffness, and its flange can carry a slab.

Exercise 1Wide or deep?

A plank is 200×50 mm. Compare its second moment of area laid flat (bending about the axis parallel to the 200 mm side) and on edge. By what factor is the on-edge orientation stiffer?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Flat: b=200, h=50: I=200⋅503/12=2.083×106 mm⁴.
  2. On edge: b=50, h=200: I=50⋅2003/12=3.333×107 mm⁴.
  3. Ratio (200/50)2=16. Same material, sixteen times stiffer, because the depth is cubed and the width only enters linearly.

03.06.title: Polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates
03.06.html:
Shafts, pipes, pressure vessels and bearings are round. Describing them in x and y makes every integral messy; in polar or cylindrical coordinates the limits become constants. The one thing to remember when you switch is the Jacobian, the factor that says how big a small coordinate box really is.

Polar coordinates

x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ. A small box dr×dθ is a curved patch of width dr and arc length rdθ, so

dA=rdrdθ.

The extra r is the Jacobian ∣∂(x,y)/∂(r,θ)∣=r. Forget it and you’ll get the area of a disc as 2πR instead of πR2.

Cylindrical and spherical

System Coordinates Volume element
Cylindrical x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ, z dV=rdrdθdz
Spherical x=ρsinϕcosθ, y=ρsinϕsinθ, z=ρcosϕ dV=ρ2sinϕdρdϕdθ

Here ϕ is measured from the z axis. Check: ∫02π​∫0π​∫0R​ρ2sinϕdρdϕdθ=34​πR3.

The polar second moment

Torsion of a shaft depends on J=∬r2dA. For a hollow circular section with outer diameter D and inner d:

J=∫02π​∫d/2D/2​r2⋅rdrdθ=32π​(D4−d4),

and the maximum shear stress under torque T is τmax​=T(D/2)/J.

Worked exampleHollow versus solid shaft

A drive shaft carries T=500 N m. Option A is hollow, D=50 mm, d=40 mm. Option B is solid with the same cross-section area, so the same mass.

  1. A: area 4π​(502−402)=706.9 mm²; J=32π​(504−404)=362265 mm⁴.
  2. A: τmax​=500000⋅25/362265=34.5 MPa.
  3. B: same area means ds​=4⋅706.9/π​=30.0 mm, so J=32π​304=79522 mm⁴.
  4. B: τmax​=500000⋅15/79522=94.3 MPa.

Same steel, same weight, and the hollow shaft runs at 37% of the stress. Material near the centre carries little torque because the stress there is small; moving it outwards, where r2 is large, pays off. That’s why bicycle frames and drive shafts are tubes.

  3. Mass =2400⋅194.2=466000 kg, about 466 t.
  4. Check with a thin-shell estimate: area 2π(10.15)2=647.3 m² times thickness 0.3 m is 194.2 m³.

03.07.title: Line integrals and work
03.07.html:
Push a crate across a floor along a winding path and the work you do depends on the path. Lift it against gravity and only the height difference matters. Line integrals make that distinction precise. They add up a field along a curve, and the question “does the path matter?” leads to potential energy and conservative forces.

Work as a line integral

A force field F(r) acting on a particle moving along a curve C does work

W=∫C​F⋅dr=∫ab​F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt,

where r(t), a≤t≤b, traces the curve. Only the force component along the motion counts, as in lesson 02.01.

Conservative fields

If F=∇ϕ for some scalar ϕ, the integral telescopes:

∫C​∇ϕ⋅dr=ϕ(rend​)−ϕ(rstart​).

The work is path independent, and around any closed loop it’s zero. In physics the potential energy is V=−ϕ, so F=−∇V. Gravity and ideal springs are conservative; friction and drag are not.

Testing for conservative

In 2D, F=(P,Q) on a region without holes is conservative exactly when

∂x∂Q​=∂y∂P​.

(Mixed partials of ϕ commute.) In 3D the condition is ∇×F=0, the subject of lesson 03.09. To find ϕ, integrate P with respect to x, then fix the “constant” (a function of y) by matching Q.

Worked examplePath matters, or not

Move from (1,0) to (0,1) (metres) along two paths: the straight line, and the quarter circle of radius 1.

Field 1: F=(2xy,x2) N. Test: ∂Q/∂x=2x=∂P/∂y, conservative with ϕ=x2y.

  1. Work =ϕ(0,1)−ϕ(1,0)=0−0=0 J on either path.

Field 2: F=(−y,x) N, a swirl. Test: ∂Q/∂x=1=−1=∂P/∂y, not conservative.

  1. Straight line r=(1−t,t): F⋅r′=(−t)(−1)+(1−t)(1)=1, so W=1 J.
  2. Quarter circle r=(cost,sint), 0≤t≤π/2: F⋅r′=sin2t+cos2t=1, so W=π/2=1.571 J.

Different paths, different work. Around the full unit circle, Field 2 does 2π J: a machine that extracts energy each lap, which is why real forces of this shape (a stirring paddle, wind in a vortex) need a power source.

Exercise 1Find the potential

Show that F=(ycosx+2x, sinx) is conservative, find ϕ, and compute the work from (0,0) to (π/2,3).

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ∂Q/∂x=cosx and ∂P/∂y=cosx: equal, so conservative.
  2. ϕ=∫(ycosx+2x)dx=ysinx+x2+g(y). Then ∂ϕ/∂y=sinx+g′(y)=Q=sinx, so g is a constant.
  3. ϕ=ysinx+x2. Work =ϕ(π/2,3)−ϕ(0,0)=3+π2/4=5.467.

03.08.title: Divergence and flux
03.08.html:
How much water flows through a pipe cross-section? How much heat leaves a hot electronics box? Both are fluxes: a field integrated over a surface. The divergence theorem says that the total flux out of a closed surface equals what’s produced inside, and applying it to a tiny box gives the conservation laws of fluid mechanics and heat transfer.

Flux through a surface

For a vector field F and a surface S with unit normal n,

Φ=∬S​F⋅ndA.

If F=ρu is a mass flux, Φ is kg/s through S. If F=q is a heat flux, Φ is watts.

Divergence

∇⋅F=∂x∂Fx​​+∂y∂Fy​​+∂z∂Fz​​.

It’s the net outflow per unit volume from an infinitesimal box: the flux out of the right face minus the flux into the left face is ∂x∂Fx​​dx⋅dydz, and the same in y and z. Positive divergence is a source, negative a sink, zero means what flows in flows out.

The divergence theorem

For a closed surface S bounding a volume V:

∬​S​F⋅ndA=∭V​∇⋅FdV.

From the theorem to conservation laws

Mass in a fixed volume changes only by flux through its boundary: dtd​∭ρdV=−∬​ρu⋅ndA. Turn the surface integral into a volume integral and, because the volume is arbitrary,

∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅(ρu)=0.

That’s the continuity equation. For an incompressible fluid it reduces to ∇⋅u=0. The same argument with energy gives the heat equation (lesson 03.14).

Worked exampleFlow through a pipe

Laminar flow in a pipe of radius R=10 mm has the parabolic profile u(r)=umax​(1−r2/R2) with umax​=0.4 m/s.

  1. Flux through the cross-section: Q=∫02π​∫0R​umax​(1−r2/R2)rdrdθ=2πumax​(2R2​−4R2​)=2π​umax​R2.
  2. Numbers: Q=2π​⋅0.4⋅0.012=6.28×10−5 m³/s =3.77 L/min.
  3. Mean velocity: Q/(πR2)=umax​/2=0.2 m/s.
  4. Divergence theorem check on the field F=(x,y,z): ∇⋅F=3, so the flux out of a sphere of radius 2 is 3⋅34​π⋅8=32π=100.5. Directly: on the sphere F⋅n=∣r∣=2, times area 16π, gives the same 32π.

Exercise 1Heat leaving a box

An electronics enclosure is a cube of side 0.2 m. Inside, components dissipate 40 W uniformly. At steady state, what’s the average heat flux through the walls? If one face is insulated, what’s the average flux through the other five?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Steady state: the total flux out equals the heat generated, 40 W (the divergence theorem with ∇⋅q equal to the volumetric heat source).
  2. Total wall area 6⋅0.04=0.24 m², so the average flux is 40/0.24=167 W/m².
  3. With one face insulated: 40/0.2=200 W/m² through the other five. The total can’t change, so the remaining faces work harder.

03.09.title: Curl and circulation
03.09.html:
Stir a cup of coffee and the fluid rotates. Pull the spoon out and a tiny paddle wheel dropped in still spins. Curl measures that local spinning, and circulation measures the total swirl around a loop. Stokes' theorem ties them together, and they explain lift on a wing, the vortices shed by a bridge, and why some force fields have a potential and others don’t.

Circulation

The circulation of a velocity field around a closed curve C is

Γ=∮C​u⋅dr.

It’s the line integral of lesson 03.07 around a loop. For a conservative field it’s zero.

Curl

∇×F=(∂y∂Fz​​−∂z∂Fy​​, ∂z∂Fx​​−∂x∂Fz​​, ∂x∂Fy​​−∂y∂Fx​​).

Its component along n is the circulation per unit area around a tiny loop perpendicular to n. In fluids, ω=∇×u is the vorticity, and for a fluid element in rigid rotation at angular velocity Ω it equals 2Ω: the paddle wheel spins at half the vorticity.

Stokes' theorem

For a surface S bounded by the curve C:

∮C​F⋅dr=∬S​(∇×F)⋅ndA.

In 2D this is Green’s theorem: ∮(Pdx+Qdy)=∬(∂x​Q−∂y​P)dA. It’s why the test in lesson 03.07 works: zero curl everywhere inside means zero circulation around every loop.

Two vortices that look alike

  • Forced vortex (rigid rotation, like a stirred cup): uθ​=Ωr. Vorticity 2Ω everywhere, and circulation grows with the enclosed area.
  • Free vortex (a bathtub drain, a tornado’s outer region): uθ​=Γ/(2πr). Vorticity zero everywhere except at the centre, yet the circulation around any loop enclosing the centre is Γ. All the curl is concentrated on the axis.

Worked exampleCirculation in a stirred tank

Fluid in a mixing tank rotates rigidly at Ω=3 rad/s: u=(−Ωy,Ωx).

  1. Curl: ∂x​uy​−∂y​ux​=Ω−(−Ω)=2Ω=6 s⁻¹.
  2. Circulation around a circle of radius R=0.5 m: speed ΩR=1.5 m/s along a length 2πR=3.14 m gives Γ=4.712 m²/s.
  3. Stokes: vorticity × area =6⋅π⋅0.25=4.712 m²/s. The same.
  4. A free vortex with that same Γ would have speed Γ/(2πr)=0.75/r m/s: 1.5 m/s at r=0.5 m, but 7.5 m/s at 0.1 m. That’s why the water near a drain spins so fast.

Exercise 1Is it rotating?

A shear flow near a wall has u=(ky,0) with k=50 s⁻¹. The streamlines are straight lines. Does a small paddle wheel placed in the flow spin? If so, which way and how fast?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Curl: ∂x​uy​−∂y​ux​=0−k=−50 s⁻¹.
  2. Nonzero vorticity, so yes: the top of the paddle wheel is pushed faster than the bottom.
  3. Negative means clockwise (for y up, x to the right), at an angular speed of half the vorticity: 25 rad/s.
  4. Straight streamlines don’t mean irrotational flow. Boundary layers are full of vorticity even though the fluid moves in straight lines.

03.10.title: Potential flow fields
03.10.html:
If a flow is both incompressible (∇⋅u=0) and irrotational (∇×u=0), its velocity is the gradient of a potential that satisfies Laplace’s equation. Laplace’s equation is linear, so you can build complicated flows by adding simple ones. That’s how the first aerodynamicists understood flow around cylinders and wings, and it still gives the right pressure distribution away from boundary layers.

Potential and stream function

Irrotational means u=∇ϕ. Incompressible then gives

∇2ϕ=∂x2∂2ϕ​+∂y2∂2ϕ​=0.

In 2D there’s also a stream function ψ with u=∂ψ/∂y, v=−∂ψ/∂x. Lines of constant ψ are streamlines, and the flow rate between two streamlines is the difference in ψ. It satisfies Laplace’s equation too.

Building blocks

Flow ψ in polar coordinates
Uniform stream, speed U Ursinθ
Source of strength m 2πm​θ
Doublet of strength κ −2πrκsinθ​
Free vortex, circulation Γ −2πΓ​lnr

Flow past a cylinder

Uniform stream plus a doublet with κ=2πUR2:

ψ=U(r−rR2​)sinθ.

ψ=0 on r=R, so the circle is a streamline: a solid cylinder. On its surface the speed is ∣uθ​∣=2Usinθ, and Bernoulli gives the pressure coefficient

Cp​=21​ρU2p−p∞​​=1−4sin2θ.

The distribution is symmetric front to back, so the net drag is zero: d’Alembert’s paradox. Real cylinders have drag because the boundary layer separates (Phase 12). Add a clockwise vortex of circulation Γ (flow left to right) and the symmetry top to bottom breaks: the flow speeds up over the top, and the cylinder gets an upward lift per unit span L′=ρUΓ (Kutta-Joukowski). That’s how a spinning ball curves.

Worked exampleA cylinder in a 10 m/s breeze

A pole of radius R=0.1 m in air at U=10 m/s, ρ=1.2 kg/m³.

  1. Fastest flow at the sides (θ=90∘): 2U=20 m/s.
  2. There Cp​=1−4=−3, so p−p∞​=−3⋅21​⋅1.2⋅102=−180 Pa.
  3. Front stagnation point: Cp​=1, p−p∞​=+60 Pa.
  4. Potential-flow drag: zero (symmetric pressure). A real pole at Re=UD/ν=10⋅0.2/1.5×10−5=1.3×105 has CD​≈1.2, a drag of 1.2⋅60⋅0.2=14.4 N per metre of height.
  5. Spin it to give Γ=4 m²/s: lift =1.2⋅10⋅4=48 N per metre. That’s the Magnus effect, used by Flettner rotor ships.

  2. θ=30∘,150∘,210∘,330∘.
  3. Between 30∘ and 150∘ (and the mirror range) the pressure is below ambient. Pressure taps at ±30∘ read the free-stream static pressure, a trick used in some flow probes.

03.11.title: Fourier series
03.11.html:
A periodic force from a cam, a gear mesh or a reciprocating engine is rarely a pure sine. Fourier’s idea was that any reasonable periodic signal is a sum of sines and cosines at whole multiples of the base frequency. That matters because linear systems respond to each sine separately: if one harmonic lands on a resonance, it can dominate the response even when it’s small in the input.

The series

For a function with period 2L:

f(x)=2a0​​+n=1∑∞​(an​cosLnπx​+bn​sinLnπx​),
an​=L1​∫−LL​f(x)cosLnπx​dx,bn​=L1​∫−LL​f(x)sinLnπx​dx.

The coefficient formulas come from orthogonality: ∫−LL​sinLmπx​sinLnπx​dx=0 for m=n. Multiply the series by one sine, integrate, and every other term vanishes. It’s the projection idea of lesson 02.07 in a space of functions.

The square wave

A square wave switching between +1 and −1 is odd, so only sines appear:

f(x)=π4​(sinx+3sin3x​+5sin5x​+…).

Two things to notice:

  1. Decay rate tracks smoothness. A jump gives coefficients falling like 1/n; a kink (continuous, slope jumps) like 1/n2; smoother still, faster. Sharp edges need high harmonics.
  2. Gibbs phenomenon. Near a jump the partial sums overshoot by about 9% of the jump, and adding terms only squeezes the overshoot closer to the jump. The peak tends to 1.179, not 1.

Parseval’s theorem

The mean square of the signal equals the sum of the squares of its harmonics:

2L1​∫−LL​f2dx=4a02​​+21​n≥1∑​(an2​+bn2​).

Energy is shared out among harmonics, which is what a power spectrum shows.

Worked exampleA cam that excites a resonance

A cam pushes a follower with a square-wave force of amplitude 100 N at 2 Hz. The follower assembly has a natural frequency of 6 Hz.

  1. Harmonics of a square wave: bn​=nπ4⋅100​ for odd n. Fundamental (2 Hz): 127.3 N. Third (6 Hz): 42.4 N. Fifth (10 Hz): 25.5 N.
  2. The third harmonic sits exactly on the 6 Hz resonance. With damping ratio ζ=0.05, the dynamic amplification at resonance is 1/(2ζ)=10, against about 1/(1−(2/6)2)=1.125 at the fundamental.
  3. Response amplitudes in force-equivalent terms: fundamental 127.3⋅1.125=143 N, third harmonic 42.4⋅10=424 N.
  4. The “small” third harmonic produces three times the motion of the fundamental, and the follower visibly vibrates at 6 Hz. Fixes: change the cam profile to a smooth one with weak third harmonic, or move the resonance.

Exercise 1The sawtooth

Find the Fourier series of f(x)=x on (−π,π), repeated periodically. How fast do the coefficients decay, and why?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. f is odd, so an​=0.
  2. bn​=π1​∫−ππ​xsinnxdx=π2​∫0π​xsinnxdx. Integrating by parts gives n2(−1)n+1​.
  3. f(x)=2(sinx−2sin2x​+3sin3x​−…).
  4. The coefficients decay like 1/n because the periodic extension jumps from π to −π at x=±π. At x=π/2 the series gives Leibniz’s π/4=1−31​+51​−….

03.12.title: The Fourier transform and FFT
03.12.html:
Measured signals aren’t formulas: they’re lists of samples from an accelerometer or a microphone. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) turns those samples into frequency content, and the fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes it in O(NlogN) operations instead of O(N2). That speed-up is why every vibration analyser, spectrum app and audio codec can work in real time.

The DFT

For N samples x0​,…,xN−1​ taken at rate fs​:

Xk​=n=0∑N−1​xn​e−2πikn/N,k=0,…,N−1.

Bin k corresponds to frequency fk​=kfs​/N. Two numbers set what you can see:

  • Resolution Δf=fs​/N=1/T, where T is the record length. To separate peaks 0.5 Hz apart, record at least 2 s.
  • Nyquist frequency fs​/2. Anything above it aliases (lesson 00.08). Only bins up to N/2 carry information for real signals.

A sine of amplitude A exactly on bin k gives ∣Xk​∣=AN/2, so the one-sided amplitude spectrum is 2∣Xk​∣/N.

Why it’s fast

Split the sum into even and odd samples:

Xk​=Ek​+e−2πik/NOk​,Xk+N/2​=Ek​−e−2πik/NOk​,

where E and O are DFTs of length N/2. One length-N transform becomes two of length N/2 plus N multiplications. Recursing gives Nlog2​N work. For N=220 that’s about 20 million operations instead of 1012.

Leakage and windows

The DFT assumes the record repeats forever. If a sine doesn’t fit a whole number of periods in the record, the repeated signal has a jump, and its energy leaks into neighbouring bins. Multiplying the record by a smooth window (Hann: wn​=sin2(πn/N)) tapers the ends to zero and confines the leakage, at the cost of a slightly wider peak. Correct the amplitude by the window’s mean (0.5 for Hann).

Worked exampleFinding the vibration in a pump

An accelerometer samples at fs​=1024 Hz for T=1 s (N=1024). The signal is 2.0 m/s² at 50 Hz (rotor imbalance) plus 0.5 m/s² at 120 Hz (vane pass) plus noise.

  1. Resolution Δf=1 Hz, Nyquist 512 Hz. Both tones sit exactly on bins 50 and 120.
  2. The FFT’s one-sided amplitudes at those bins come out at 2.00 and 0.50 m/s² (the code checks it).
  3. Now the rotor speeds up slightly to 50.5 Hz, halfway between bins. Without a window the peak reads only 1.28 m/s², spread over many bins. With a Hann window (corrected by its mean of 0.5) the peak reads 1.70 m/s², and the leakage ten bins away is about 80 times smaller.
  4. Lessons: choose T for the resolution you need, use a window for amplitudes between bins, and don’t trust a single bin’s amplitude to better than about 15% without one.

Exercise 1Plan a measurement

You want to resolve two gear-mesh tones at 312 Hz and 313.5 Hz and capture harmonics up to 2 kHz. What minimum sample rate and record length do you need, and how many samples is that?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Harmonics to 2 kHz need fs​>4 kHz; with an anti-alias filter margin, use about 5 kHz (5120 Hz is a common choice).
  2. To separate peaks 1.5 Hz apart you need Δf well below 1.5 Hz; with a Hann window the main lobe is about 4Δf wide, so take Δf=0.25 Hz, meaning T=4 s.
  3. Samples: N=fs​T=5120⋅4=20480, or round up to 215=32768 (6.4 s) for a radix-2 FFT.

03.13.title: Classifying PDEs
03.13.html:
Partial differential equations describe fields that change in space and time: temperature, displacement, pressure, velocity. Second-order linear PDEs come in three families, and the family decides everything: what boundary and initial data you need, how information travels, and which numerical method will work. The test is a discriminant, just like for conic sections.

The three types

For Auxx​+Buxy​+Cuyy​+(lower-order terms)=0, compute B2−4AC:

B2−4AC Type Prototype Behaviour
<0 elliptic Laplace uxx​+uyy​=0 equilibrium; every point feels every boundary point
=0 parabolic heat ut​=αuxx​ diffusion; smooths out, infinite propagation speed, one direction in time
>0 hyperbolic wave utt​=c2uxx​ waves; information travels at finite speed along characteristics

For the heat equation, take y=t: A=α, B=C=0, so B2−4AC=0. For the wave equation, A=c2, C=−1: B2−4AC=4c2>0.

What each type needs

  • Elliptic: boundary conditions all around a closed region, no initial data. Steady heat conduction, static elasticity, potential flow.
  • Parabolic: an initial condition plus boundary conditions. Transient heat, diffusion of a pollutant, consolidation of soil.
  • Hyperbolic: initial displacement and velocity plus boundary conditions. Vibrating strings and beams, acoustics, supersonic flow.

Characteristics

For hyperbolic equations there are curves along which information travels. For utt​=c2uxx​ they’re the lines x±ct=const: a disturbance at one point affects only the region between those lines, its domain of influence. Numerical methods must respect this: a time step that lets information jump further than one grid cell per step is unstable (the CFL condition, lesson 04.15).

Type can change: compressible flow

Small disturbances in steady 2D compressible flow satisfy (1−M2)ϕxx​+ϕyy​=0, where M is the Mach number. Then B2−4AC=−4(1−M2):

  • M<1: elliptic. A subsonic body is felt upstream; air starts moving aside before the nose arrives.
  • M>1: hyperbolic. Disturbances stay inside a Mach cone of half-angle μ=arcsin(1/M), and nothing upstream knows the body is coming.

Worked exampleClassify and interpret

  1. 3uxx​+2uxy​+uyy​=0: B2−4AC=4−12=−8. Elliptic.
  2. uxx​−4uxy​+4uyy​=0: 16−16=0. Parabolic.
  3. A flat plate in an airflow at M=2: 1−M2=−3, so B2−4AC=12>0, hyperbolic. Mach angle μ=arcsin(1/2)=30∘.
  4. The same plate at M=0.5: B2−4AC=−3, elliptic. The flow field is smooth everywhere and extends upstream.
  5. Characteristics for case 3: slopes dy/dx=±1/M2−1​=±0.577, lines at ±30∘. The Mach waves.

Exercise 1The Tricomi equation

The Tricomi equation yuxx​+uyy​=0 models transonic flow. Where in the plane is it elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=y, B=0, C=1, so B2−4AC=−4y.
  2. y>0: negative discriminant, elliptic (subsonic region).
  3. y=0: parabolic (the sonic line).
  4. y<0: hyperbolic (supersonic region).
  5. A single equation can change type across the domain, which is why transonic flow is hard to compute: the solver has to switch between equilibrium-like and wave-like behaviour.

03.14.title: The heat equation
03.14.html:
Take a hot steel rod out of a furnace and clamp both ends in cold blocks. How long until the middle is safe to touch? The heat equation answers it, and its solution by separation of variables shows a pattern you’ll meet again and again: the answer is a sum of modes, each decaying at its own rate, and after a while only the slowest one matters.

Derivation in one paragraph

Energy balance on a slice of rod, area A, thickness dx: the rate of change of stored heat equals the net conducted inflow. Stored heat is ρcTAdx; conducted flux is q=−k∂T/∂x (Fourier, lesson 03.02). The divergence argument of lesson 03.08 in 1D gives

∂t∂T​=α∂x2∂2T​,α=ρck​.

α is the thermal diffusivity: about 1.2×10−5 m²/s for steel, 9.7×10−5 for aluminium, 1.1×10−4 for copper.

Separation of variables

Rod of length L, ends held at T=0, initial temperature T0​(x). Try T=X(x)Θ(t):

αΘΘ′​=XX′′​=−λ.

The left side depends only on t and the right only on x, so both equal a constant. With X(0)=X(L)=0, the solutions are Xn​=sinLnπx​ with λn​=(nπ/L)2, and Θn​=e−αλn​t. Superpose and match the initial condition with a Fourier sine series (lesson 03.11):

T(x,t)=n∑​bn​sinLnπx​e−α(nπ/L)2t.

For a uniform initial temperature T0​, bn​=4T0​/(nπ) for odd n.

Mode n decays like e−n2t/τ

The time constant of the slowest mode is

τ1​=π2αL2​.

Mode 3 decays 9 times faster, mode 5 25 times faster. After about 0.2τ1​ the profile is essentially a single sine arch shrinking exponentially. Doubling the length quadruples the time: diffusion time scales with length squared.

Worked exampleWhen can you touch the rod?

A 0.5 m steel rod (α=1.2×10−5 m²/s) at 100 °C has its ends clamped at 0 °C (above the room temperature baseline). Treat the sides as insulated.

  1. Time constant τ1​=0.25/(9.87⋅1.2×10−5)=2111 s =35.2 min.
  2. Centre temperature from the series: 92.6 °C after 10 min, 54.3 °C after 30 min, 23.1 °C after 60 min, 4.2 °C after 120 min.
  3. One-mode estimate for late times: Tc​≈π400​e−t/τ1​. At 60 min: 127.3e−1.706=23.1 °C, matching the series to 3 digits.
  4. To reach 45 °C (comfortable to touch): t=τ1​ln(127.3/45)=36.6 min.
  5. A copper rod (α=1.11×10−4) has τ1​=3.8 min and gets there in under 4 minutes.

Exercise 1Scale it up

A 2 m aluminium bar (α=9.7×10−5 m²/s) has the same end conditions. What’s its slowest time constant, and how does it compare with the 0.5 m steel rod?

03.15.title: The wave equation
03.15.html:
Pluck a guitar string and two things happen at once: a shape travels along the string at a fixed speed, and the string rings at a set of definite pitches. Both views come from the same equation. The wave equation governs strings, axial vibrations of rods, sound in pipes, and (in more dimensions) acoustics and seismic waves.

Derivation

A string under tension T with mass per length μ. For a small piece dx with small slope, the vertical tension components differ by T∂2u/∂x2dx. Newton’s second law:

μdx∂t2∂2u​=T∂x2∂2u​dx⟹∂t2∂2u​=c2∂x2∂2u​,c=T/μ​.

The same equation holds for longitudinal waves in a rod with c=E/ρ​ (about 5100 m/s in steel) and sound in air with c=γRT​ (343 m/s at 20 °C).

Travelling waves: d’Alembert

Any function of x−ct or of x+ct solves the equation. With initial shape f(x) and zero initial velocity,

u(x,t)=21​[f(x−ct)+f(x+ct)]:

the initial shape splits into two halves that run apart at speed c. At a fixed end the wave reflects upside down.

Standing waves: modes

With fixed ends at x=0 and x=L, separation of variables gives modes sinLnπx​cosωn​t with

fn​=2Ln​μT​​,n=1,2,3,…

Whole-number multiples of the fundamental: a harmonic series, which is why strings sound musical. A string plucked at a fraction a of its length has mode amplitudes proportional to sin(nπa)/n2. Modes with a node at the pluck point are missing.

Worked exampleTuning a guitar string

A string of length L=0.65 m and μ=0.4 g/m is tensioned to T=70 N.

  1. Wave speed c=70/4×10−4​=418.3 m/s.
  2. Fundamental f1​=c/(2L)=418.3/1.3=321.8 Hz.
  3. The target is E4 at 329.6 Hz. Since f∝T​, the tension needs to rise by (329.6/321.8)2=1.049, to 73.4 N.
  4. Plucked at a=1/4: relative harmonic amplitudes sin(nπ/4)/n2 normalised to the first are 1, 0.35, 0.11, 0, 0.04, 0.04. The 4th harmonic is missing; pluck near the bridge (small a) for a brighter sound with more high harmonics.
  5. A pulse takes L/c=1.55 ms to run the length of the string. One period of the fundamental is 2L/c=3.11 ms: out to the far end and back.

Exercise 1A steel rod rings

A 1 m steel rod, free at both ends, rings in longitudinal vibration. With E=210 GPa and ρ=7850 kg/m³, what’s the wave speed and the fundamental frequency? (For free-free ends, fn​=nc/(2L) as well.)

  1. c=E/ρ​=210×109/7850​=5172 m/s.
  2. f1​=c/(2L)=2586 Hz.
  3. That’s the high “ting” of a struck bar. Halving the length doubles the pitch, so a tuning fork maker adjusts frequency by grinding length.

03.16.title: The Laplace equation
03.16.html:
Wait long enough and a heated plate stops changing: every point settles at the temperature its surroundings dictate. That steady state obeys Laplace’s equation, the most common elliptic PDE in engineering. It also governs potential flow (lesson 03.10), electrostatics, and seepage through soil. You’ll solve it two ways: with a series, and with the five-point stencil and an iterative solver from Phase 02.

From heat to Laplace

Set ∂T/∂t=0 in the 2D heat equation:

∇2T=∂x2∂2T​+∂y2∂2T​=0.

With an internal heat source q˙​ (W/m³) it becomes Poisson’s equation ∇2T=−q˙​/k.

Two properties worth knowing

  • Mean value property: the value at any point equals the average over any circle around it. So the solution has no bumps or dips inside.
  • Maximum principle: the maximum and minimum occur on the boundary. A plate with edges between 0 and 100 °C is between 0 and 100 °C everywhere inside. Useful as a sanity check on any numerical solution.

Series solution on a square

Unit square, top edge at T0​, other edges at 0. Separation of variables (as in 03.14, but with sinh in y):

T(x,y)=n odd∑​nπsinhnπ4T0​​sin(nπx)sinh(nπy).

The five-point stencil

On a grid with spacing h, replace each second derivative by a central difference:

h2Ti+1,j​+Ti−1,j​+Ti,j+1​+Ti,j−1​−4Ti,j​​=0.

Each interior value is the average of its four neighbours: the discrete mean value property. Writing this for every node gives a sparse SPD system (lesson 02.14) with five nonzeros per row. Gauss-Seidel solves it by sweeping “replace each value by the average of its neighbours” until nothing changes; SOR or CG (02.15) do it much faster. The error is O(h2).

Worked exampleThe centre of a hot-topped plate

A square plate with its top edge at 100 °C and the other three at 0 °C.

  1. Superposition trick: rotate the problem four times so each edge takes a turn at 100 °C. Adding the four solutions gives a plate with all edges at 100 °C, whose solution is 100 °C everywhere. By symmetry each of the four contributes equally at the centre, so the centre is exactly 100/4=25 °C.
  2. The series confirms it: T(0.5,0.5)=25.00 °C. Also T(0.5,0.75)=54.1 °C and T(0.5,0.25)=9.5 °C.
  3. A 41×41 grid with SOR gives the centre to within 0.01 °C of 25 (the code checks it).
  4. Halving h cuts the error at (0.5,0.75) by about 4: second-order accuracy.

Exercise 1Heat through the edges

In the hot-topped plate (unit square, top at 100 °C, other edges at 0 °C, conductivity k), which edges carry most of the heat out, and how much heat per unit thickness leaves through the bottom? Differentiate the series term by term at y=0 and integrate over x.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. All the heat enters through the top and leaves through the other three edges. The side edges meet the hot edge at the top corners, where the temperature jumps from 100 °C to 0 °C, so the gradients there are unbounded and the sides carry by far the most heat.
  2. At y=0: ∂T/∂y=∑nπ4T0​​sinhnπnπ​sinnπx. Integrating sinnπx over [0,1] gives 2/(nπ), so the bottom flux is k∑nodd​nπsinhnπ8T0​​≈22.06k W per metre of thickness. The first term alone gives 22.05.
  3. The total through the sides is infinite in this idealised model: the corner jump is not physical. A real plate has a thin transition zone at each corner, which makes the total finite but still dominated by the sides.

03.17.title: Boundary conditions
03.17.html:
A PDE alone has infinitely many solutions. The boundary conditions pick the one that matches your physical problem, and getting them wrong is the most common modelling error in simulation. There are three kinds, each with a physical meaning and a standard way to put it into a finite-difference or finite-element model.

The three types

Name Prescribes Heat transfer meaning Mechanics meaning
Dirichlet the value u fixed temperature (wall clamped to a cold block) fixed displacement (support)
Neumann the normal derivative ∂u/∂n fixed heat flux; zero for insulation or symmetry applied traction (load)
Robin a combination au+b∂u/∂n convection: −k∂T/∂n=h(T−T∞​) elastic support (spring foundation)

Two practical rules:

  • A pure-Neumann problem (only fluxes given) determines the solution only up to a constant, like an unsupported structure (lesson 02.06). At least one Dirichlet or Robin condition pins it down.
  • Symmetry planes are Neumann conditions with zero flux. Model half or a quarter of a symmetric part and save the computation.

The Biot number

For convection at a solid’s surface, compare the internal conduction resistance L/k with the external convection resistance 1/h:

Bi=khL​.

If Bi≪1, the solid is nearly isothermal and the surface sits close to the interior temperature; if Bi≫1, the surface is pulled almost to T∞​ and the Robin condition behaves like Dirichlet.

Boundary conditions in finite differences

  • Dirichlet: just set the boundary node’s value.
  • Neumann and Robin: add a ghost node outside the boundary and use a central difference for the derivative. That keeps second-order accuracy; a one-sided difference drops to first order.

Worked exampleHeat loss through a wall in winter

A 0.2 m brick wall (k=1.4 W/(m K)) has its inner face held at 20 °C (Dirichlet) and its outer face exposed to wind at −5 °C with h=25 W/(m² K) (Robin).

  1. Resistances in series per square metre: conduction L/k=0.1429 m² K/W, convection 1/h=0.04 m² K/W.
  2. Heat flux q=25/(0.1429+0.04)=136.7 W/m².
  3. Outer surface temperature: Ts​=−5+q/h=−5+5.47=0.47 °C. Just above freezing.
  4. Bi=hL/k=3.57: neither limit. Treating the outer face as Dirichlet at −5 °C would overestimate the loss to 25/0.1429=175 W/m², 28% too high.
  5. The code solves the same problem with finite differences and a ghost node; with 11 nodes it matches the exact flux to machine precision, because the exact solution is linear.

Exercise 1Insulate the wall

You add 60 mm of insulation (k=0.035 W/(m K)) on the outside of the brick wall. What’s the new heat flux and the new outer surface temperature?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Insulation resistance 0.06/0.035=1.714 m² K/W.
  2. Total resistance 0.1429+1.714+0.04=1.897 m² K/W, so q=25/1.897=13.2 W/m², about a tenth of before.
  3. Outer surface: Ts​=−5+13.2/25=−4.47 °C, almost the air temperature. With insulation, the Biot number of the whole wall is large and the outer face behaves almost like a Dirichlet boundary.

03.18.title: Laplace transform
03.18.html:
The Laplace transform turns linear differential equations with constant coefficients into algebra. Derivatives become multiplications by s, initial conditions come along automatically, and the ratio of output to input becomes a transfer function whose poles tell you at a glance whether a system is stable, how fast it responds and how much it overshoots. It’s the language of control engineering (Phase 18).

Definition and the key rule

F(s)=L{f(t)}=∫0∞​f(t)e−stdt.

Integrating by parts gives the rule that does all the work:

L{f′(t)}=sF(s)−f(0),L{f′′(t)}=s2F(s)−sf(0)−f′(0).

A small table

f(t) F(s)
1 (unit step) 1/s
e−at 1/(s+a)
sinωt ω/(s2+ω2)
e−atcosωt (s+a)/((s+a)2+ω2)
δ(t) (impulse) 1

Solving an ODE

For mx¨+cx˙+kx=F(t) starting at rest, transform term by term:

(ms2+cs+k)X(s)=F(s)⟹G(s)=F(s)X(s)​=ms2+cs+k1​.

To get x(t) back, split X(s) into partial fractions and read each term off the table.

Poles tell the story

The roots of the denominator, the poles, are s=−ζωn​±iωn​1−ζ2​ with ωn​=k/m​ and ζ=c/(2km​). The real part sets the decay rate, the imaginary part the oscillation frequency. All poles in the left half-plane means stable.

Two shortcuts:

  • Final value theorem: limt→∞​x(t)=lims→0​sX(s), if the system is stable.
  • Step overshoot for a second-order system: Mp​=e−ζπ/1−ζ2​, peaking at tp​=π/ωd​.

Worked exampleStep response of a suspension model

m=1 kg, c=4 N s/m, k=20 N/m, hit by a 10 N step force.

  1. X(s)=s(s2+4s+20)10​.
  2. Poles: s=0 and s=−2±4i. So ωn​=20​=4.472 rad/s, ζ=4/(220​)=0.447, ωd​=4 rad/s.
  3. Final value: lims→0​sX(s)=10/20=0.5 m, the static deflection F/k.
  4. Partial fractions: X(s)=s0.5​−(s+2)2+160.5(s+2)+0.25⋅4​, so x(t)=0.5[1−e−2t(cos4t+0.5sin4t)].
  5. Overshoot e−0.447π/0.894=e−π/2=20.8% at tp​=π/4=0.785 s: the peak is 0.604 m.

Exercise 1Pick the damper

For the same m=1 kg and k=20 N/m, what damping c limits the step overshoot to 5%?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Mp​=e−ζπ/1−ζ2​=0.05 gives ζπ/1−ζ2​=ln20=2.996.
  2. Square and solve: ζ2(π2+2.9962)=2.9962, so ζ=2.996/9.870+8.974​=0.690.
  3. c=2ζkm​=2⋅0.690⋅4.472=6.17 N s/m.

03.19.title: Systems of ODEs and phase planes
03.19.html:
A pendulum’s state is two numbers, angle and angular velocity. Plot one against the other and every possible motion becomes a curve in the phase plane. Equilibria are points, oscillations are loops, and linear algebra (the eigenvalues of a Jacobian) tells you whether nearby motions spiral in, spiral out, or escape. It’s the qualitative toolkit for nonlinear mechanics.

First-order form

Any ODE system can be written as y˙​=f(y). The pendulum θ¨+2ζω0​θ˙+ω02​sinθ=0 becomes, with y=(θ,ω),

θ˙=ω,ω˙=−ω02​sinθ−2ζω0​ω.

At every point of the plane, f is an arrow: the direction field. Trajectories follow the arrows and never cross (uniqueness).

Equilibria and linearisation

Equilibria are where f=0: for the pendulum, θ=0 (hanging) and θ=π (inverted). Near an equilibrium y∗, let y=y∗+η:

η˙​≈Jη,J=∂y∂f​​y∗​.

The solution is a combination of eλt terms, with λ the eigenvalues of J (lesson 02.09):

Eigenvalues Picture Stability
real, both negative node stable
real, opposite signs saddle unstable
complex, negative real part spiral in stable
complex, positive real part spiral out unstable
purely imaginary centre neutral (linear test inconclusive)

The pendulum’s two equilibria

  • At θ=0: J=(0−ω02​​1−2ζω0​​), eigenvalues −ζω0​±iω0​1−ζ2​. A stable spiral for 0<ζ<1.
  • At θ=π: cosπ=−1 flips the sign: J=(0ω02​​1−2ζω0​​), eigenvalues real with opposite signs. A saddle: balance a broomstick and it falls.

Without damping, energy is conserved and trajectories are level curves of E=21​ω2−ω02​cosθ. The curve through the saddle, the separatrix, divides swinging from going over the top: ω=±2ω0​cos(θ/2).

Worked exampleWill the swing go over the top?

A pendulum of length L=1 m hangs at rest. You hit it to give the bob a speed v0​.

  1. ω0​=g/L​=3.132 rad/s.
  2. Undamped separatrix at θ=0: ω=2ω0​=6.264 rad/s, so v0​=6.26 m/s at the bob.
  3. Energy check: to reach the top the bob climbs 2L=2 m, needing 21​v02​=2gL, so v0​=4gL​=6.26 m/s. The phase-plane and energy answers agree.
  4. Linearised at the bottom with ζ=0.1: eigenvalues −0.313±3.116i. Each swing period (2π/3.116=2.02 s) the amplitude shrinks by e−0.313⋅2.02=0.53.
  5. At the top: eigenvalues of (09.81​1−0.626​) are 2.84 and −3.46. A small tilt grows by a factor e every 0.35 s.

Exercise 1Classify a predator-prey model

For x˙=x(1−y), y˙​=y(x−1), find the equilibria and classify them.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Equilibria: (0,0) and (1,1).
  2. J=(1−yy​−xx−1​).
  3. At (0,0): J=diag(1,−1), eigenvalues ±1, a saddle.
  4. At (1,1): J=(01​−10​), eigenvalues ±i, a linear centre. The linear test is inconclusive, but this system has a conserved quantity x−lnx+y−lny, so the orbits really are closed loops.

03.20.title: Green's functions intuition
03.20.html:
If a structure is linear, you only need to know its response to a single point load. Any other load is a sum of point loads, so the response is a sum (an integral) of point-load responses. The point-load response is the Green’s function. Engineers know it as the influence line, and it’s the idea behind the boundary element method and much of signal processing.

The idea

For a linear operator L (for a beam, Lu=EIu′′′′) with boundary conditions, the Green’s function G(x,ξ) solves

LG(x,ξ)=δ(x−ξ),

the response at x to a unit point load at ξ. Then for a distributed load q:

u(x)=∫G(x,ξ)q(ξ)dξ.

It’s superposition taken to the limit. In time, the same idea is the impulse response h(t), and y=∫h(t−τ)f(τ)dτ is a convolution.

The simply supported beam

For a beam of length L and a unit load at ξ, with x≤ξ and b=L−ξ:

G(x,ξ)=6EILbx​(L2−b2−x2),

and by symmetry (swap the roles) for x>ξ. Integrate it against a uniform load w and you recover the textbook midspan deflection 5wL4/(384EI).

Maxwell’s reciprocal theorem

G(x,ξ)=G(ξ,x): the deflection at A due to a load at B equals the deflection at B due to the same load at A. It follows from the symmetry of the stiffness operator, the continuous version of K=KT from Phase 02. It’s also a practical trick: to find how a load anywhere affects one point, put a single load at that point and measure the deflected shape.

Worked exampleA steel beam under two load cases

An IPE 200 section (I=1943×104 mm⁴, E=200 GPa, so EI=3.886×106 N m²) spans L=4 m, simply supported.

  1. Point load P=10 kN at midspan: δ=PL3/(48EI)=104⋅64/(48⋅3.886×106)=3.43 mm. This is PG(L/2,L/2).
  2. Uniform load w=5 kN/m: δ=∫0L​G(L/2,ξ)wdξ=5wL4/(384EI)=4.29 mm. The code does the integral numerically and matches.
  3. Influence line: move the 10 kN load to ξ=1 m and read the midspan deflection off G(2,1): 2.36 mm. Reciprocity says a load at midspan deflects the point x=1 m by the same 2.36 mm.
  4. Both load cases together: 3.43+4.29=7.72 mm. Linearity lets you add them; a span/deflection ratio of 4000/7.72=518 passes a typical L/300 serviceability limit.

Exercise 1Where should the jack go?

On the same beam, a hydraulic jack pushes up with force F at x=1 m to cancel the midspan deflection from the 5 kN/m uniform load. Using the influence value from the example, how big must F be?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Midspan deflection from the uniform load: 4.29 mm down.
  2. A unit upward force at x=1 m lifts midspan by G(2,1)=2.36×10−7 m/N (from 2.36 mm per 10 kN).
  3. F=4.29×10−3/2.36×10−7=18.2 kN.
  4. Reciprocity check: that’s the same as asking how much a load at midspan would deflect the jack point. Placing the jack at midspan instead would need only 4.29/3.43×10=12.5 kN, because the beam is most flexible there.
